extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent practitioners, and legal readers drafting or litigating historic UK patents and copyright (early 19th-century context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and form-language for petitioning for a royal patent and for the letters patent themselves, together with remedial and procedural standards for copyright infringement suits, equitable injunctions, and evidentiary/pleading practice in the courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for copyright infringement (threefold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedies for an infringement of the copyright of a book may be: I. By a suit for penalties. II. By an action on the case for damages. III. By proceedings in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates and treats each remedy separately and explains their scope and purpose (penalties as statutory punishments, actions for damages to compensate the injured proprietor, and equity for injunctions to restrain irremediable injury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit for penalties under the Statute of Anne
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties given by the Statute of Anne against piracy: every offender shall forfeit the book and every sheet (to be delivered to the proprietor to be made waste paper) and forfeit a monetary penalty (a penny, now three pence) for every sheet found in his possession, one moiety to the Queen and the other to the informer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties are recoverable in actions in the courts at Westminster; however no penalties can be imposed unless the title of the book before publication be entered in the register book of the Company of Stationers. Time for bringing penalties has been limited by statute (noted as twelve months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action on the case for damages (common-law remedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proprietor of a book may maintain a special action on the case for any injury received by a piracy of his book and recover damages the jury think proper to assess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action for damages may be maintained even if the book was not entered at Stationers' Hall or did not have the author's name affixed; the statute's penalties are cumulative and do not oust the common-law action. Double costs are given to a plaintiff successful in a special action on the case; defendants recover costs if plaintiff is nonsuited or discontinues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry at Stationers' Hall for imposition of statutory penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: No penalties under the statute can be imposed on anyone unless the title of the book before its publication be entered in the register book of the Company of Stationers; consent to publish (assignments) must also be entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry serves as notice/warning to the public so they may not ignorantly incur forfeitures; however, lack of entry does not necessarily preclude a common-law action for damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for bringing statutory actions/penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The time limited for bringing penalties (and altered in several statutes) is stated to be twelve months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The limitation period is repeatedly noted in the chapter as applying to statutory proceedings; practitioners must observe statutory time-bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings in an action for infringing a copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: In pleadings for infringement there is nothing to distinguish them from actions on the case in general; the plea allowed by the statutes is the general issue 'Not Guilty' with liberty to give special matter in evidence under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations and precedents are cited; usual practice includes adducing the books in evidence for comparison. Procedural consequences (costs awards) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence — comparison of works and same errors as proof of piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are usually adduced in evidence so that by comparison the court and jury may see that one is an infringement of another; the circumstance of the same errors being found in two publications on the same subject is considered evidence of a piracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lord Chancellor or a master may be directed to compare the works; comparison is a central evidentiary method in infringement disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity/injunctions — necessity of clear title or possession (and colourable title)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity originally required a clear legal title to grant injunctions to restrain infringement; later practice relaxed this so injunctions may be granted and continued until hearing upon possession alone, although where the title is doubtful and there is no possession, an injunction may be refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chancery refused assistance absent clear title; later practice permits injunctions on possession under colour of title; if proprietor has permitted others to publish without interposition, equity will often decline to interpose until legal title is established at law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit and assignment evidence required to support a bill for injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: To support the bill of an assignee of a copyright there must be an affidavit that the assignment was made in writing; a general affidavit stating the copy had been purchased was held insufficient if it did not state purchase from the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits as to facts filed after answer may be read at the hearing, but an affidavit as to title cannot be received after the answer. Specificity and proof of a written assignment are required to support equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court practice on hearing motions for injunctions — examination and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: On motion to protect a right (book or patent) the Lord Chancellor will read the works or refer to a master to examine whether the books are the same or differ and in what respect; he will then dissolve or continue the injunction or make such order as meets the justice of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If convenient, the Lord Chancellor prefers to compare the works himself; a master's report may be used; procedure is summary and discretionary aimed at preventing irremediable injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will not assist where publication is unlawful at law
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity will not protect or decree an account for a publication which an action at law could not maintain; in such cases equity will not decree an account even on submission in the answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity 'loathes all impurity' and will not aid wrongdoers or protect unlawful publications; practitioners must ensure the subject matter is lawful at law to expect equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent petition — required allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Form of the petition for patent must state that the petitioner, after considerable application and expense, hath invented or found out [title of invention], that he is the true and first inventor, and that it hath not been made or used by any other person to his knowledge or belief; prayer that Majesty grant letters patent for sole working, making, selling, using and exercising the invention for the term of fourteen years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specimen petition language is provided; the petition should assert novelty, first invention, public benefit, and the exact relief (letters patent for a term, territories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit to support the patent petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit language: that after considerable application and expense the deponent hath invented/found out [title], believes it will be of general benefit and advantage, is the true and first inventor thereof, and that the same hath not been made or used by any other person to his knowledge or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The affidavit must be sworn (sample marks 'Sworn at the Public Office...'); specificity that the invention is first and not previously used is critical to support the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and scope of the letters patent (grant language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent grant a special licence, full power, sole privilege and authority to the patentee and assigns to make, use, exercise and vend the invention within England, Wales, Berwick-upon-Tweed (and optionally colonies) in such manner as the patentee in his discretion thinks meet, during the term of fourteen years; they command all persons and officers not to molest the patentee in the due use or exercise of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specimen patent contains customary grant language, territorial scope, exclusive privileges, and commands to officers; practitioners should follow the formula to ensure the intended monopoly and protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions rendering the letters patent void (novelty/contrary to law clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided that if at any time the grant is contrary to law, prejudicial or inconvenient to subjects in general, or that the invention is not a new invention or not invented by the petitioner, then upon signification by the Crown or six or more of the privy council these letters patent shall forthwith cease, determine and be utterly void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent grants include express provisos allowing revocation if not new or contrary to public interest; also the patent shall not be construed to give privilege to use or imitate any invention 'heretofore been invented or found out' and publicly used by other subjects to whom like letters patent have been already granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on transfers/assignments and public subscriptions (limit to five persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee shall make any transfer or assignment or declare any trust of the patent to any number of persons exceeding the number of five, or open any book for public subscription by more than five persons, or act as a corporate body or divide benefits into shares exceeding five, then the letters patent shall utterly cease, determine and become void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grant contains an explicit limitation on how the patentee may distribute or corporate-ize the grant (likely to prevent de facto monopolies or corporate misuse); compliance is mandatory or the patent may be voided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to particularly describe and enroll the invention in Chancery
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee shall not particularly describe and ascertain the nature of his invention and in what manner it is to be performed by an instrument in writing under his hand and seal, and cause the same to be enrolled in the High Court of Chancery within next and immediately after the date of the letters patent, then the letters patent and liberties shall utterly cease, determine and be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification/enrolment requirement is a condition precedent to the patent's validity: the invention must be described in writing, sealed and enrolled in Chancery within the statutory/required time, or the grant is void.
